node.label: John Lewis Gaddis
node.date_label: Strategies of Containment (1982) · We Now Know: Rethinking Cold War History (1997) · The Landscape of History (2002)
node.description: A historian of the Cold War and strategy whose selected writings revisit historical explanations as evidence and perspectives change. In a 1998 primary essay he connects the opening of former communist archives with revisions to Cold War interpretation, while admitting that no historical representation can recover everything. He argues for greater attention to ideology and offers a separate, controversial account of nuclear weapons as both stabilizing and prolonging the conflict. Those are Gaddis’s interpretations, not settled judgments about comparative regimes or the whole Cold War.

incident_edges.relationship: Reassesses Cold War political power through ideology, legitimacy and newly available evidence.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary essay’s opening and second numbered argument, read. His comparative claims about regime performance and Soviet legitimacy remain attributed and disputable. This does not treat access to some archives as complete evidence.

incident_edges.relationship: Argues that nuclear deterrence could both stabilize crises and prolong the Cold War by masking other dimensions of state power.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary essay’s third argument explicitly distinguishes these two effects. It is a contested historical interpretation, not a generic military appointment arrow or a validated counterfactual for every crisis.
